claims.text: Targeted grain-boundary segregation produces ultrathin passivating intergranular films.
These intergranular films govern both structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Cr, Al, or other selected species segregate to nanoscale interfaces during synthesis.
The resulting passivation layers are coherent and self-healing.
The passivation layers retard grain-boundary diffusion.
The passivation layers inhibit rapid oxidation.
Changing cooling rate or chemical precursors can promote targeted grain-boundary segregation.
Oxidation and grain growth are active degradation mechanisms near 800°C in an oxidizing atmosphere.
The segregated element forms a stable protective oxide or nitride film at grain boundaries.
The protective film reduces atomic mobility at grain boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary atomic mobility retards grain coarsening.
The protective film limits oxygen ingress and chemical degradation.
Lower intergranular diffusion and oxidation preserve structural integrity and phase composition at high temperature.
A segregation-promoted alloy will exhibit slower grain growth than a homogeneous baseline alloy.
A segregation-promoted alloy will exhibit reduced oxidation depth relative to the baseline.
A segregation-promoted alloy will retain mechanical properties better after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The beneficial effect is expected around 700–900°C in oxidizing environments where grain-boundary diffusion is significant.
The beneficial effect may fail when the protective film destabilizes or spalls, or when the alloy chemistry does not permit effective segregation.
The magnitude of stabilization depends on the alloy system and dopant level.
Inherent sluggish diffusion may compete with grain-boundary segregation as a stabilization mechanism in high-entropy systems.
